title.en: The Fomor's Stake at Chess and the Broken Bread
title.zh: 弗莫爾的棋局賭注與碎麵包

region.en: Cave by the western sea, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭西海岩洞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. V, eBook #14465

summary.en: Storm-bound in a sea cave, Diarmuid and Grania host Ciach the Fierce One of the Fomor; at chess Diarmuid wins, and the Fomor stakes Grania for his winnings. Grania, jealous of the touch, stabs Diarmuid's thigh — and he makes an end of the Fomor and will not speak to her. From the Quarrel come the famous farewell-laments of Diarmuid and Grania, and the sign to Finn of broken faith: henceforth broken bread, not whole, is left behind.
summary.zh: 風暴困於海洞，迪爾穆德與格拉尼亞款待弗莫爾悍者基亞赫；棋局迪爾穆德得勝，弗莫爾竟以格拉尼亞作為賭注索取。格拉尼亞妒火中燒，刺傷迪爾穆德大腿——他誅殺弗莫爾後拒與她言語。由此衍生迪爾穆德與格拉尼亞著名的離別哀歌，以及向芬恩示忠的標記——此後留下的不再是整塊麵包，而是碎屑。

sensitivity.note: Chess as a binding game with persons as stake is the fixed otherworld-gamble motif (cf. Midir and Etain, Finn and the chessboard oracles); Diarmuid's leaving bread as a fidelity-sign to Finn is the tracking device of the pursuit narrative. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: One night while they were there a great storm came on, so that they went into the far part of the cave. But bad as the night was, a man of the Fomor, Ciach, the Fierce One, his name was, came over the western ocean in a currach, with two oars, and he drew it into the cave for shelter. And Diarmuid bade him welcome, and they sat down to play chess together. And he got the best of the game, and what he asked as his winnings was Grania to be his wife, and he put his arms about her as if to bring her away. And Grania said: "I am this long time going with the third best man of the Fianna, and he never came as near as that to me." And Diarmuid took his sword to kill Ciach, and there was anger on Grania when she saw that, and she had a knife in her hand and she struck it into Diarmuid's thigh. And Diarmuid made an end of the Fomor, and he said no word to Grania, but ran out and away through the storm.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the break of day she overtook him, and after a while they heard the cry of a heron: "Tell me that, Grandson of Duibhne, to whom I gave my love." "O Grania, daughter of the High King, woman who never took a step aright, it is because she was frozen to the rocks she gave that cry. O Grania of the beautiful hair, though you are more beautiful than the green tree under blossom, your love passes away as quickly as the cold cloud at break of day... I lost my people by you, and my lord, and my large bright ships on every sea; I lost my treasure and my gold; it is hunger you gave me through your love." And Grania said: "O Diarmuid of the face like snow, the sound of your voice was dearer to me than all the riches of the leader of the Fianna. The love-spot on your forehead is better to me than honey in streams... O Diarmuid of the beautiful hands, take me now the same as before; it was with me the fault was entirely; give me your promise not to leave me." But Diarmuid said: "How can I take you again, you are a woman too fond of words; one day you give up the Head of the Fianna, and the next day myself, and no lie in it." They came then to a place where there was a cave, and water running by it, and they stopped to rest; and Grania said: "Have you a mind to eat bread and meat now, Diarmuid? Give me a knife, so, till I cut it." "Look for the knife in the sheath where you put it yourself." She saw then that the knife was in his thigh where she had struck it, for he would not draw it out himself; so she drew it out then, and that was the greatest shame that ever came upon her.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: They stopped then in the cave. And the next day when they went on again, Diarmuid did not leave unbroken bread like he had left every other day as a sign to Finn that he had kept his faith with him, but it was broken bread he left after him. And they went on wandering after that, all through Ireland, hiding from Finn in every place, sleeping under the cromlechs, or with no shelter at all, and wherever they went Finn would follow them, for he knew by his divination where they went; but one time he made out they were on a mountain, for he saw them with heather under them, and it was beside the sea they were, asleep on heather that Diarmuid had brought down from the hills for their bed; and so he went searching the hills and did not find them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. V-VI; not verbatim.

title.en: Grania's Sleep-Songs over the Wandering Bed
title.zh: 格拉尼亞的搖籃曲與流浪之床

region.zh: 愛爾蘭都柏林郡埃達山（霍斯）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. VI, eBook #14465

summary.en: Watched over by the sleep of Diarmuid, Grania sings her songs of the sleep in the South and the North and the West and the East — then rouses him: the stag is not asleep, the hornless doe cries after her fawn, the bog lark is not sleeping between the streams. In a cave of Beinn Edair an old woman dips her cloak in the sea and lies of frost and rivers to hold them for Finn; Grania tastes salt on the cloak and Diarmuid arms — and Angus Og's boat carries them away in the nick of night.
summary.zh: 守著迪爾穆德的酣眠，格拉尼亞唱起南、北、西、東四方名人酣睡之歌——隨即喚醒他：雄鹿未眠，無角母鹿啼喚花斑幼鹿，雲雀仍在溪澗間守望。埃達山洞中，老嫗以海水蘸濕斗篷、謊稱嚴寒冰封以拖住二人等芬恩到來；格拉尼亞舌試斗篷嚐出鹹味，迪爾穆德披掛而起——安古斯·奧格之舟恰於深夜接應他們脫險。

sensitivity.note: Grania's sleep-song and rousing-song are quoted whole through the cycle and are among the most anthologised Fenian lyrics; the wet-cloak betrayal test (tasting salt) is a countersign motif. Pin at Beinn Edair cave tradition.

passages.text: And Grania would be watching over Diarmuid while he slept, and she would make a sleepy song for him: "Sleep a little, a little little, for there is nothing at all to fear, Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne; sleep here soundly, soundly, Diarmuid, to whom I have given my love. It is I will keep watch for you, grandchild of shapely Duibhne; sleep a little, a blessing on you, beside the well of the strong field; my lamb from above the lake, from the banks of the strong streams. Let your sleep be like the sleep in the South, of Dedidach of the high poets, the time he took away old Morann's daughter, for all Conall could do against him. Let your sleep be like the sleep in the North, of fair comely Fionnchadh of Ess Ruadh, the time he took Slaine with bravery as we think, in spite of Failbhe of the Hard Head. Let your sleep be like the sleep in the West, of Aine, daughter of Gailian, the time she went on a journey in the night with Dubhthach from Doirinis, by the light of torches. Let your sleep be like the sleep in the East, of Deaghadh the proud, the brave fighter, the time he took Coincheann, daughter of Binn, in spite of fierce Decheall of Duibhreann."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. VI; not verbatim.

passages.text: And then to rouse him she would make another song: "Caoinche will be loosed on your track; it is not slow the running of Caoilte will be; do not let death reach to you, do not give yourself to sleep for ever. The stag to the east is not asleep, he does not cease from bellowing; the hornless doe is not asleep, crying after her speckled fawn; she is going over the bushes, she does not sleep in her home. The cuckoo is not asleep, the thrush is not asleep, the tops of the trees are a noisy place; the duck is not asleep, she is made ready for good swimming; the bog lark is not asleep to-night on the high stormy bogs; the sound of her clear voice is sweet; she is not sleeping between the streams."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. VI; not verbatim.

passages.text: One time they were in a cave of Beinn Edair, and there was an old woman befriending them and helping them to keep a watch; and one day she chanced to go up to the top of Beinn Edair, and saw an armed man coming towards her, and did not know him to be Finn: "It is looking for a woman I am come, and for a woman's love. And will you do all I will ask you?" "I will do that," she said, for she thought it was her own love he was asking; and she told him where Diarmuid was hiding. She dipped her cloak in the sea-water before she went into the cave, and made a complaint against the cold: "Cold, cold, cold to-night is the wide plain of Lurg; the snow is higher than the mountains, the deer cannot get at their share of food... Ice is heaped up in every ford; it is for that I am saying and ever saying 'Cold.'" And when she was gone, Grania took hold of the cloak she had left there and put her tongue to it, and found the taste of salt water on it: "My grief, Diarmuid, the old woman has betrayed us. And rise up now, and put your fighting suit upon you." And no sooner were they outside than they saw Finn and the Fianna of Ireland coming towards them; then Diarmuid saw a little boat at hand in the shelter of the harbour, and they knew it was Angus was in it, that had come again to help them to escape from Finn, and they went back with him for a while to Brugh na Boinne.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. VI; not verbatim.

title.en: Finn's Nurse and the Spearing through the Drowned Leaf
title.zh: 芬恩的奶母與洞穿枯葉之矛

region.en: Land of Promise, western ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 應許之地，西海（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. VII, eBook #14465

summary.en: Beaten in Alban, Finn sails to the Land of Promise for his nurse, for it is not possible to put Diarmuid down by any strength of an army unless enchantment would put him down. Under a Druid mist she rises on a blast of Druid wind over the hunting Diarmuid with a drowned leaf, pierced like a mill-quern, and aims deadly spears through the hole — until Diarmuid, lying on his back, casts the Red Spear through the hole itself and the hag falls dead on the spot.
summary.zh: 阿爾巴受挫，芬恩遠航應許之地求助於奶母——「非魔力不能制服迪爾穆德」。她以德魯伊霧隱身，乘魔風升至打獵的迪爾穆德頭頂，持一片葉孔如磨盤的枯葉，穿孔擲出致命之矛——迪爾穆德仰臥舉紅矛，一擲洞穿葉孔，巫嫗當場斃命。

sensitivity.note: The nurse-enchantress of the Land of Promise is Finn's female counter-gift from the Sidhe (paralleling Manannan's fostering of Diarmuid); the millstone-holed leaf is one of the cycle's signature marvel-weapons. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: And after that, Finn went out again on the sea, and his people with him, and there is no word of them till they came to the Land of Promise where Finn's nurse was. And when she saw Finn coming she was very joyful before him. And Finn told her the whole story from beginning to end, and the cause of his quarrel with Diarmuid; and he said it was to ask an advice from her he was come, and that it was not possible to put him down by any strength of an army, unless enchantment would put him down. "I will go with you, and I will do enchantment on him."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: And when they came to Brugh na Boinne, the nurse put a Druid mist around Finn and the Fianna, the way no one could know they were there. Now the day before that, Osgar had parted from Diarmuid, and Diarmuid was out hunting by himself. That was shown to the hag, and she took a drowned leaf having a hole in it, like the quern of a mill, and she rose with that by her enchantments on a blast of Druid wind over Diarmuid, and began to aim at him through the hole with deadly spears, till she had done him great harm, for all his arms and his clothing, and he could not make away he was so hard pressed. And every danger he was ever in was little beside that danger. And it is what he thought, that unless he could strike the old woman through the hole that was in the leaf, she would give him his death there and then. And he lay down on his back, and the Gae Dearg, the Red Spear, in his hand, and he made a great cast of the spear, that it went through the hole, and the hag fell dead on the spot. And he struck off her head and brought it back with him to Angus Og.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. VII; not verbatim.

title.en: Peace with Finn and the Settling of Rath Grania
title.zh: 與芬恩議和與格拉尼亞堡的安定

region.en: Rath Grania, Ceis Corainn, Co. Kerry, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡格拉尼亞堡（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. VII, eBook #14465

summary.en: With Finn's nurse dead, Angus Og goes mediator: to Finn, to the High King, and home to Diarmuid, who will make peace only on conditions — his father's district of Ui Duibhne free of Finn's hunting and the King's tribute, Dumhais in Leinster, and Ceis Corainn as a marriage portion with the King's daughter. The terms are granted, sixteen years of hiding are forgiven, and at Rath Grania Grania bears him four sons and a daughter, richer in gold and cattle than any man living.
summary.zh: 巫嫗既死，安古斯·奧格充當調停人：先見芬恩，再見至高王，最後回到迪爾穆德處。後者僅在特定條件下方肯議和——父親封地伊·迪夫涅免於芬恩狩獵與王室貢賦、倫斯特之杜馬伊斯、以及隨王室之女作嫁妝的凱斯·科雷恩。條件獲准，十六年藏匿既往不咎；格拉尼亞在堡中為他誕下四子一女，金銀牛羊之富冠絕當世。

sensitivity.note: The peace-conditions are a land-grant legal episode (éiric and marriage-portion vocabulary); the sixteen-year term of hiding is the cycle's fixed chronology before the Boar of Beinn Gulbain. Pin symbolic at traditional Rath Grania.

passages.text: And the next morning early, Angus rose up, and he went where Finn was, and he asked would he make peace with Diarmuid, and Finn said he would. And then he went to the King of Ireland to ask peace for Diarmuid, and he said he would agree to it. And then he went back to where Diarmuid and Grania were, and asked him would he make peace with the High King and with Finn. "I am willing, if they will give the conditions I will ask. The district my father had, that is, the district of Ui Duibhne, without right of hunting to Finn, and without rent or tribute to the King of Ireland; and with that the district of Dumhais in Leinster, for they are the best in Ireland, and the district of Ceis Corainn from the King of Ireland as a marriage portion with his daughter; and those are the conditions on which I will make peace with them."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. VII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Angus went with that news to where the King of Ireland was with Finn, and they gave him all those conditions, and they forgave him all he had done through the whole of the time he had been in his hiding, that was sixteen years. And the place Diarmuid and Grania settled in was Rath Grania, in the district of Ceis Corainn, far away from Finn and from Teamhair; and Grania bore him children there, four sons and one daughter. And they lived there in peace, and the people used to be saying there was not a man living at the same time was richer as to gold and to silver, as to cattle and to sheep, than Diarmuid.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. VII; not verbatim.
